title: That Wedding Videographer Podcast
author: Jason Hunter and Danny Rizzo
description: A podcast for wedding videographers covering filming techniques, business growth, pricing, marketing and industry insights through real conversations and practical advice from two working UK wedding filmmakers.

episodes.title: Ep. 120 - YOU ARE TOO OLD TO FILM WEDDINGS... Apparently
episodes.summary: Danny and Jason react to a post claiming Gen Z couples should only hire Gen Z videographers, and argue that connection with clients is human, not generational.

episodes.title: Ep. 119 - The Industry Responded: Videographers vs Content Creators Part 2
episodes.summary: After a big response to episode 118, the hosts go through the comments, discuss deliverables models and pressure at the lower end of the market, and plan to bring content creators onto the show.

episodes.title: Ep. 118 - Content Creators Vs Wedding Videographers - What's The Difference?
episodes.summary: The hosts respond to a content creator's claim that only creators capture candid moments. Their answer: both capture the same moments; the real difference is post-production, with creators sending raw footage within 48 hours and videographers curating a film built to last.

episodes.title: Ep. 117 - Should You Ever Discount Your Prices?
episodes.summary: Jason explains how his view on discounting moved from a flat no to context-based decisions around venue distance, weekday dates and outsourced editing. Danny reveals he runs three seasonal pricing brochures.

episodes.title: Ep. 116 - Is TikTok the Most Untapped Platform for Wedding Videographers Right Now?
episodes.summary: TikTok strategy for wedding videographers, including behind-the-scenes and talking-head content, plus the announcement of the That Wedding Videographer Summit 2027 in Glasgow.

episodes.title: Ep. 115 - How to Run a Wedding Film Business Alongside a Full-Time Job (Without Losing Your Mind)
episodes.summary: Guest Andy of House of Tattersall Films shoots 20 to 25 weddings a year while holding a full-time marketing job, outsourcing editing for six to eight week turnarounds.

articles.question: What is the difference between a wedding content creator and a videographer?
articles.metaDescription: Wedding filmmakers Jason Hunter and Danny Rizzo explain the real difference between a content creator and a videographer: what happens after the day.
articles.intro: A wedding content creator and a wedding videographer often film the same moments; the difference is what you get afterward. On That Wedding Videographer Podcast, working filmmakers Jason Hunter and Danny Rizzo explain that content creators hand over raw, phone-shot footage within about 48 hours, while videographers curate, edit and pair the footage with audio to build a film designed to last. Neither is wrong, but they are different products.

sections.heading: The claim that started the argument
sections.body:
The episode was prompted by a post from a wedding content creator suggesting that only content creators capture the candid stuff: the fleeting glances, the atmosphere, the conversations in the corner. Videographers, the post implied, just produce beautiful cinema.

Danny and Jason push back hard on that. In their experience, and in the work of most wedding videographers they know, the candid moments are the whole point. Capturing the speech reactions, the quiet moment between the couple and the grandparents on the dance floor is exactly what a good wedding film is made of.

The hosts explain that framing it as candid-versus-cinematic is a false choice. It misrepresents what videographers deliver and, more importantly, it confuses couples who are trying to decide what to book.

sections.heading: The real difference happens after the wedding
sections.body:
Here's the distinction the hosts land on: it's not about the day, it's about post-production.

A content creator typically shoots on a phone, moves fast, and sends the couple raw or lightly trimmed clips within roughly 48 hours. The value is speed and immediacy. You have something to post on Instagram before the honeymoon.

A videographer takes the same moments and does something different with them. They curate, choosing the shots that tell the story. They shape the footage, cutting for pacing and emotion. They pair moments with audio, so the vows play over the first look and the best man's line lands over the reaction shot. And they build something designed to last, a film the couple will watch on anniversaries rather than scroll past in a week.

Same raw material. Different craft, different timeline, different result.

sections.heading: What couples should ask before booking either
sections.body:
Because both services can look similar on a sales page, the hosts' framing suggests a few questions couples should ask:

- **What exactly do I receive, and when?** Raw clips in 48 hours is a different deliverable from an edited film in six to eight weeks. Both are legitimate. Know which you're paying for.
- **Is the footage edited and paired with audio?** This is the core of the videographer's job and the thing you can't easily do yourself afterward.
- **How long is this meant to be watched for?** Social content is for this week. A wedding film is for the next thirty years.
- **Can I have both?** Many couples do book both, and the hosts see no conflict in that. The mistake is booking one and expecting the other.

The hosts explain that this clarity protects the couple's expectations and protects both professionals from bad reviews caused by a mismatch.

sections.heading: Stay in your lane, and stop selling by tearing others down
sections.body:
The episode ends with a message to the industry rather than to couples. Both services capture the same moments and both produce something of genuine value. Content creators offer speed and social-ready clips. Videographers offer curation and longevity. Neither needs to undermine the other to make its case.

Danny and Jason's call is for professionals to stay in their lane: sell what you do well, describe it honestly, and don't market by implying the other side doesn't capture real moments. That kind of post might get engagement, but it misleads couples and cheapens the whole category.

The response to this episode was big enough that the hosts recorded a follow-up going through the comments and invited content creators onto the show. For anyone deciding what to book, the takeaway is simpler: figure out whether you want fast raw footage, a crafted film, or both, and hire accordingly.

keyTakeaways: Content creators and videographers usually capture the same candid moments; the difference is in post-production.
Content creators typically deliver raw or lightly trimmed footage within about 48 hours, ideal for social media.
Videographers curate, edit and pair footage with audio to make a film built to be rewatched for years.
Couples should ask exactly what they'll receive and when, and can book both services if they want both outcomes.
Both are legitimate products; professionals shouldn't sell one by misrepresenting the other.

faq.q: Do I need both a content creator and a videographer for my wedding?
faq.a: Only if you want both outcomes: quick social-ready clips within a couple of days and a fully edited film later. The hosts see no conflict in booking both, as long as you know what each delivers.

faq.q: How fast does a wedding content creator deliver footage?
faq.a: Typically within about 48 hours, according to the episode. Videographers take longer because they edit, curate and pair the footage with audio.

faq.q: Do wedding videographers capture candid moments?
faq.a: Yes. Jason and Danny argue that candid reactions, glances and conversations are the core of a good wedding film, not something only content creators capture.

articles.sourceNote: Based on That Wedding Videographer Podcast episode 118, "Content Creators Vs Wedding Videographers - What's The Difference?", released August 20, 2026, hosted by Jason Hunter and Danny Rizzo.
